title: Syngas Production from Electrochemical CO2 Reduction on Copper Oxide Electrodes in Aqueous Solution
abstract: Electrochemical CO2 reduction to value-added chemicals and fuels using renewable energy represents a promising strategy for reducing CO2 emissions and achieving effective energy storage. In this work, nano-sized CuO catalysts were prepared by using the homogeneous precipitation method for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO. The CO2 reduction studies combined with the characterization results show that structureactivity relationships of the CuO catalysts depend on the calcination temperature. The as-synthesized CuO catalysts calcined at different temperatures are capable of reducing CO2 to generate syngas with tunable CO/H2 ratios of 1 : 2 to 2 :1. The desired CuO-400 catalyst exhibits good morphology, small particle size, and enriched oxygen-vacancy defects and, therefore, shows good performance for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO. Under the given potential of 0.93 V vs. RHE, CuO400 exhibits good reduction activity and selectivity with a great electrochemically active surface area normalized CO partial current density of 1.44 mA/cm and a high CO faradaic efficiency of 48.2%. The deactivation of CuO-400 in the longterm test is associated with the increase in particle size, the reduction of CuO to Cu2O and metallic Cu, and the coverage of surface active sites by the formed carbonate species. Our findings indicate that CuO catalysts with tunable physicochemical properties are promising candidates for electrochemical CO2 reduction to produce syngas.

sections.heading: Syngas Production from Electrochemical CO2 Reduction on Copper Oxide Electrodes in Aqueous Solution
sections.text:
Xi Yao, Yafei Guo,* Bingqian Liu, Puyao Wang, Jian Sun, Weiling Li, and Chuanwen Zhao*[a]
Electrochemical CO2 reduction to value-added chemicals and fuels using renewable energy represents a promising strategy for reducing CO2 emissions and achieving effective energy storage. In this work, nano-sized CuO catalysts were prepared by using the homogeneous precipitation method for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO. The CO2 reduction studies combined with the characterization results show that structureactivity relationships of the CuO catalysts depend on the calcination temperature. The as-synthesized CuO catalysts calcined at different temperatures are capable of reducing CO2 to generate syngas with tunable CO/H2 ratios of 1 : 2 to 2 :1. The desired CuO-400 catalyst exhibits good morphology, small particle size, and enriched oxygen-vacancy defects and, therefore, shows good performance for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO. Under the given potential of 0.93 V vs. RHE, CuO400 exhibits good reduction activity and selectivity with a great electrochemically active surface area normalized CO partial current density of 1.44 mA/cm2 and a high CO faradaic efficiency of 48.2%. The deactivation of CuO-400 in the longterm test is associated with the increase in particle size, the reduction of CuO to Cu2O and metallic Cu, and the coverage of surface active sites by the formed carbonate species. Our findings indicate that CuO catalysts with tunable physicochemical properties are promising candidates for electrochemical CO2 reduction to produce syngas.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Global warming and energy crisis are emerging as two significant issues in the 21st century. CO2 capture and utilization (CCU) has been regarded as an effective strategy to mitigate the impacts.[1] In particular, electrochemical reduction of CO2 (ERC) to value-added chemicals and fuels using renewable energy could be an attractive route to achieve carbon neutrality.[2] The products of the ERC process include CO, methane, ethylene, formic acid, methanol, and higher alcohols, depending on the multiple-electron transfer pathways.[3] Significantly, both the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) are involved in the ERC process. Combined with CO2RR and HER, the ERC process will produce syngas with tunable CO/H2 ratios, which is an important feedstock for synthesizing chemicals via the Fischer-Tropsch (F T) process.[4]
Single-atom catalysts of Ag and Au have been identified as highly active for ERC to CO, in terms of their high CO selectivity over H2. Nevertheless, the large-scale applications of the precious metals have been restricted by their high cost and limited reserves.[5] In this respect, transition metals have been considered as potential alternatives to precious metal catalysts for ERC. Particularly, copper-based catalysts have been recog-
nized as active for ERC to varieties of products.[6] However, the high potential needed for ERC and the limited selectivity toward the desired products remain two challenges for copper-based catalysts.[7] One promising approach is the synthesis of oxidederived (OD) Cu catalysts with tunable surface properties. Wang et al. reported that copper nanowire arrays (Cu NAs) were capable of reducing CO2 to produce syngas with a high syngas faradaic efficiency (>70%) at a low potential ( 0.5 V vs. RHE).[4a] Another efficient strategy is to dope the bulk Cu with a singleatom metal to form bimetallic catalysts such as Cu In, Cu Sn and Cu Pd.[8] Yoo et al. prepared highly selective Cu Sn bimetallic catalysts which were capable of electrochemically reducing CO2 to CO with a high FECO of 98.6% at 0.45 V vs. RHE. In addition, the electrochemical performance of the catalysts depended on the composition and nanoscale geometry effects.[9]
Apart from OD nanostructured Cu and copper bimetallic catalysts, CuOx also exhibits high activity for electrochemical CO2-to-CO conversion.
[10] Catalytic activity and selectivity of CuOx catalysts for ERC have been documented to rely on various factors, including structural configuration, morphology, crystal facets, particle size and roughness.[11] Regulating surface morphology and particle size has been perceived as an efficient path to improved ERC performance. The release of CO from the surface of catalyst has been identified as the limiting step in ERC to CO. Tuning the surface morphology of catalysts could facilitate the release of CO and therefore promote CO formation rate.[12] On the other hand, particle size effects will determine the distribution of products. The decrease in particle size will facilitate CO formation and promote HER as well.[13] Huang et al. fabricated CuO with tunable morphology by controlling the configuration of raw materials and reaction temperature in a template-assisted water-bath process. The desired CuO nanowires (NWs) showed high activity toward ERC with great FECO (~20%) and FEH2 (>40%) at 0.697 V vs. RHE.[10] Calcination temperature is also an important factor influencing the morphology and particle size of the CuO nanostructures, in addition to the water-bath temperature and configuration of raw materials. Whereas the effect of calcination temperature on the structure and ERC performance of CuO electrocatalyst remains unknown yet.
Herein, we reported the preparation of CuO nanoparticles (NPs) by template-assisted homogeneous precipitation method for ERC. Results have evidenced that the structure-propertyactivity relationships of the CuO NPs depended on calcination temperature. Besides, the stability and deactivation of the CuO NPs in ERC process have also been illustrated.

sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
CuO NPs were prepared by the homogeneous precipitation method using polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP) as template. Schematic illustration of the fabrication process of the nanostructured CuO is presented in Scheme 1. The CuCl2 · 2H2O precursor and the PVP template are dissolved to form a uniform mixture. Ammonia solution (NH3 ·H2O) is then added into the mixture to promote hydrolyzation-precipitation to form the Cu2Cl(OH)3 and [Cu(NH3)4(OH)2] intermediates. Then, rapid nucleation occurs to promote the formation of [Cu(NH3)4(OH)2] with the addition of NaOH solution, and the formed intermediates are regularly attached to the surface of the PVP template. The samples are then subjected to drying and calcination in air stream, during which the formed Cu2Cl(OH)3 and [Cu(NH3)4(OH)2] intermediates are transformed into Cu(OH)2. Subsequently, the Cu(OH)2 intermediates are decomposed and the template is removed, so that the nanostructured CuO with tunable size can be produced.[14]
The as-synthesized CuO catalysts were characterized by different techniques. Figure 1 shows the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the CuO NPs calcined at different temperatures. The XRD patterns show diffraction peaks associated with crystalline CuO (PDF#05-0661) in the wide 2θ range of 32.4°–72.3°. The diffraction peaks at 35.4° and 38.6° are assigned to the (002) and (111) crystal planes of CuO. In addition to the specific peaks for the crystalline CuO (PDF#05-0661), additional diffraction peaks can also be observed at 16.1° and 17.6° on the XRD
profiles of the CuO-200 and CuO-300 catalysts. The CuCl2 · 2H2O precursor has been reported to be subjected to hydrolysis during solvothermal synthesis to form Cu2Cl(OH)3.
[14a] The thermogravimetric (TG) and differential thermal analysis (DTA) curves in published work indicated that Cu2Cl(OH)3 started to decompose at 260–320 °C.[14b,c] As a result, the diffraction peaks observed at 16.1° and 17.6° for CuO-200 and CuO-300 can thus be attributed to the undecomposed Cu2Cl(OH)3 intermediate. The diffraction peaks match well to the standard JCPDS card of Cu2Cl(OH)3 (PDF#87-0679), which has also demonstrated the presence of Cu2Cl(OH)3 intermediate. It is worth mentioning that the presence of Cu2Cl(OH)3 intermediate in CuO-200 and CuO-300 might adversely affect their electrochemical performance. With the increase of calcination temperature, the width of the strong peaks at 35.4° and 38.6° decreases and the peak intensity increases, indicating that CuO exhibits better crystallinity at higher calcination temperatures.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images in Figure 2 evidence that the surface morphology of the CuO catalysts varies with calcination temperature. As indicated in Figure 2, CuO-200 represents the one-dimensional nanowires (1D NWs) structure with massive microspherical particles attached to the surface of NWs. The 1D NWs are due to the undecomposed Cu2Cl(OH)3 intermediate, while the microspherical particles are

Hence, the CuO-300 and CuO-400 samples are consisted of many microspherical particles, and the CuO NPs are uniformly distributed. Obvious grain sintering can be observed as the calcination temperature further increases to 500 °C, and spherical CuO NPs begin to aggregate to form large blocks.
High resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images in Figure 3 reveal the evolution of the surface morphology of the CuO catalyst with the increasing calcination temperature (1D NWs @ 200 °C!3D NPs @ 300–400 °C!large blocks @ 500 °C). HRTEM images of the different samples show lattice
fringes with average d-spacing of 0.254 and 0.231 nm corresponding to the (002) and (111) crystal facets of CuO. Particle size distributions of CuO-300 and CuO-400 are also described in Figure 3. It is noted that the particle sizes of CuO-300 and CuO400 are in the ranges of 9–17 nm and 12–28 nm. Their average particle sizes are estimated as 12.2�0.6 nm and 20.4�1.4 nm, respectively. Thus, both the surface morphology and the particle size depend on the calcination temperature, and this will further affect the ERC performance of the CuO catalysts.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) studies of the CuO catalysts are performed and the results are presented in Figure 4. XP profiles for Cu 2p of the different CuO catalysts are shown in Figure 4(a). Two dominating characteristic peaks for Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2 can be observed at 954.0 eV and 934.0 eV with a peak separation of 20.0 eV, confirming that Cu (II) is the chemical valence state for copper species.[10] As indicated in Figure 4(b), three split peaks can be resolved from the O 1s profiles at the binding energies of 529.7 eV, 531.1 eV and 532.0 eV, which are associated with lattice oxygen (Olat), oxygen vacancies (OVs) and adsorbed oxygen (Oads), respectively. [16] Figure 4(c) shows the distribution of oxygen species in the different CuO catalysts. The oxygen species in CuO-200 are primarily derived from the undecomposed Cu2Cl(OH)3 intermediate. It is evident that the proportions of Oads and OVs decrease with the increasing calcination temperature from 300 °C to 500 °C. Meanwhile, the proportion of Olat tends to increase with the increase in calcination temperature. A higher calcination temperature will trigger the transformation of Oads and OVs to Olat, and therefore will affect the distribution of oxygen species. Similar findings have also been reported for manganese oxide catalysts.[17] Previous research has indicated that OVs play important roles in activating and reducing CO2 over metal oxide catalysts to facilitate the formation of the desired products.[18] The transformation of Oads and OVs to Olat might depress the catalytic performance of metal oxide

The cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests were performed in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte under different scan rates of 5–50 mV/s in the non-Faradaic region. The obtained CV curves are plotted in Figure S1. The average current density of the samples measured under different scan rates can be calculated. A plot of average current density (j) as a function of scan rate (ν) then yields a straight line and the slope gives the electrical double-layer capacitance (Cdl). Figure 5 shows that the Cdl values of CuO-200, CuO-300, CuO-400, and CuO-500 are 244.58, 146.19, 100.41 and 186.43 μF/cm2, respectively. Electrochemically active surface areas (ECSA) of the CuO samples are calculated to normalize the current density to reveal their specific activities.
Figure 6 shows the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves of the samples tested in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution. The onset potentials of CuO-200, CuO-300, CuO-400, and CuO500 are determined as 0.287, 0.599, 0.354 and 0.630 V vs. RHE, respectively. Compared to CuO-300 and CuO-500, CuO-400 shows a much lower CO2RR onset potential. At the applied potential of 0.93 V vs. RHE, the ECSA normalized current density increases first and then decreases. CV tests were performed in both N2- and CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution to further analyze the HER performance of the catalysts, and the CV curves are presented in Figure S2. The ECSA normalized current densities of the samples tested in the N2-saturated electrolyte are very close to those of the catalysts tested in the CO2saturated electrolyte, indicating that the catalysts favor both the CO2RR and HER processes. The observed characteristic peaks in the applied potential range should be associated with the reduction of CuO.
The ECSA normalized CO partial current density and overpotential in the Tafel region are employed to calculate the Tafel slopes. Figure 7(a) shows the Tafel plots of the different CuO catalysts. The Tafel slopes of the catalysts are determined as 81.7, 115.2, 69.7 and 135.6 mV/dec, respectively. Notably, the desired CuO-400 catalyst exhibits the lowest Tafel slope, as an indicative of intrinsically better activity. The change of turnover
frequency (TOF) with the increasing calcination temperature is shown in Figure 7(b). TOFCO increases first and then decreases with the increases in calcination temperature. CuO-400 possesses the maximum TOFCO of 516 h
1, implying that the sample exhibits the highest activity and fastest kinetics for CO production. Furthermore, diagrams of electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) are provided in Figure S3 to calculate the charge transfer resistance (Rct). Our experimental results indicate that the Rct values for the four CuO catalysts tested in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte are 18.79, 7.90, 10.47 and 16.67 ohms, respectively. In particular, CuO-400 shows the minimum Rct, as an indicative of smaller impedance, lower polarization resistance and relatively faster kinetics in CO2RR. In addition, the EIS diagrams indicate that the ERC process at high applied potentials is jointly controlled by the charge transfer in high frequency region (kinetic control) and the diffusion process in low frequency region (mass transfer control).
Figure 8 presents the FEs and ECSA normalized partial current densities of the gaseous and liquid products of the samples tested under the different applied potentials. Our experimental findings indicate that the detected gaseous and liquid products involve CO, H2, CH3OH and C2H5OH, and their total FEs range from 40% to 84%, depending on the different samples and applied potentials. The remaining FE might be associated with other products such as C2H4 and HCOOH, which cannot be detected due to the limitation of chromatographic column. Amongst the different catalysts, CuO-400 owns the highest total FEs (62%–77%) under the different applied potentials. The desired CuO-400 sample also exhibits the highest FECO values. When the applied potential is fixed at 0.93 V vs. RHE, FECO increases first and then decreases with the increasing calcination temperature. It is observed that the ECSA normalized CO partial current density (jCO-ECSA) increases first and then decreases with the increasing temperature. The CuO-400 sample shows the best CO selectivity with the highest FECO of 48.2%. It is noticed that the ratio of CO/H2 is tunable in the range of 1 :2–2 :1 with the increasing calcination temperature from 200 °C to 400 °C.

For the desired CuO-400 catalyst, as the applied potential changes from 0.13 to 0.93 V vs. RHE, FECO increases from 25.4% to 48.2% and FEH2 decreases from 27.0% to 21.1%. The ECSA normalized CO partial current density (jCO-ECSA) increases with the change of potential, while jH2-ECSA increases first and then decreases. The sample exhibits the best catalytic performance towards CO2 reduction with the maximum FECO of 48.2% and the greatest jCO-ECSA of 1.44 mA/cm
2 under the applied potential of 0.93 V vs. RHE. Notably, by regulating the applied potential in the range of 0.13~ 0.93 V vs. RHE, the ratio of CO/H2 can also be adjusted in the range of 1 :2–2 :1. Tailoring the composition of syngas is critically important for the synthesis of downstream products: e.g., CO/H2 =1 :2 for methanol production,[20] CO/H2 =2 :1 for Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, [21] and CO/H2 =1 :1 for dimethyl ether production. [4a] Hence, electrochemical CO2 reduction could be promising alternatives to coal gasification and natural gas reforming for efficient syngas production.[22]
Under a low calcination temperature of 200 °C, the Cu2Cl(OH)3 intermediate can hardly be completely decomposed, and the active CuO species available for CO2 reduction are limited. Hence, the catalytic activity of CuO-200 is poor. As the calcination temperature rises to 300–400 °C, the intermediate starts to decompose to produce CuO NPs of small particle size.
Decreased particle size is suggested to increase the ratio of surface atoms to bulk ones, and more oxygen defect sites may be exposed for facilitated CO2 adsorption and activation. Copper-based nanostructures with smaller particle sizes favor the formation of syngas, whereas NPs with greater particle sizes encourage the formation of CH4 and C2+ products.
[23] Oxygen defects play positive roles in regulating the electronic properties and electrochemical activities of metal oxides catalysts for promoted CO2 activation.
[18b] The enhanced reduction activity and selectivity of CuO-300 and CuO-400 should therefore be associated with the minimized particle size and enriched oxygen-vacancy defects. A high calcination temperature for the CuO-500 catalyst has resulted in grain sintering and particle agglomeration. This will further trigger the loss of active oxygen defects and the activation of CO2 over the catalyst will be hampered. As a result, the CuO-500 catalyst exhibits rather poor catalytic activity and selectivity.
Repeated tests have been carried out in 0.1 M CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution to evaluate the stability of the desired CuO-400 catalyst. The change of ECSA normalized total current density versus time is plotted in Figure 9(a). Fluctuation of current can be observed as potential is applied to the electrode in the initial stage. As electrolysis continues, the charge transfer process is stabilized and the current density stays stable at 3.29–3.51 mA/cm2.[10,24] At 130–140 min, the CuO-400 catalyst starts to deactivate, as indicated by the change of current density. Overall, the current density of CuO-400 drops more than 70% within the first 10 minutes and then the sample retains stable catalytic activity within 2 h.
The changes in FEs of CO and H2 and their ECSA normalized partial current densities are illustrated in Figure 9(b). As electrochemical CO2 reduction proceeds, both FECO and jCO-ECSA increase first and then decrease. The low FECO within the initial 30 min might be ascribed to the fluctuation in current density. As the electrode is applied with a high negative potential, HER produces considerable tiny bubbles and the surface of the working electrode will be covered by large bubbles due to bubble coalescence. These have resulted in the decline in ECSA normalized total current density.[10] The favored HER in the initial stage has also been evidenced by the great FEH2 and jH2ECSA. The sample then maintains stable activity towards CO2RR until FECO and jCO-ECSA decline to 15.3% and 0.26 mA/cm
2 at 120– 150 min, as an indicative of catalyst deactivation.
Figure S4 shows the color of the electrode changes from black to red after the long-term CO2 reduction test. The red electrode might be associated with Cu2O and metallic Cu, signaling the deactivation of the sample in the long-term CO2 reduction test. The fresh and spent samples are characterized by different techniques to confirm catalyst deactivation and to illustrate the underlying mechanism. XRD profiles in Figure 10 show that the fresh CuO-400 presents obvious diffraction peaks for CuO (PDF#05-0661). For the spent sample after the CO2 reduction test, the diffraction peaks observed at the 2θ angle of 36.5°, 42.4° and 61.5° are assigned to Cu2O (PDF#65-3288). Besides, the diffraction peaks for Cu (PDF#89-2838) can also be observed at 43.4°, 74.2° and 89.9°. These indicate that CuO has been partially reduced to Cu2O and metallic Cu during the long-
term CO2 reduction test. The spent CuO-400 sample shows a broader peak width and lower peak intensity for the strong peaks at 35.4° and 38.6°, as an indicative of crystallinity attenuation after CO2 electrochemical reduction.
FT-IR spectrum of the spent CuO-400 catalyst is shown in Figure S5. The peaks at 3328 and 1657 cm 1 correspond to the OH stretching and bending vibration due to the presence of water or the bonded OH on CuO.[25] The peaks observed at 2883 and 2973 cm 1 can be attributed to the symmetrical and anti-symmetric stretching vibration of C H.[26] The peaks centered at 879, 1087 and 1380 cm 1 are assigned to the outof-plane bending, symmetrical and anti-symmetric stretching vibration of carbonate species.[27] The formed carbonate species might cover the active sites for CO2 activation and would adversely affect the electrochemical performance. The peak at 1045 cm 1 corresponds to the C O C stretching vibration mode. Two bands at 432 and 618 cm 1 associated with the Cu(II) O and Cu(I) O stretching vibration mode can also be observed, indicating the presence of CuO and Cu2O species. [28]

The present Cu2O phase in the spent catalyst also evidences catalyst deactivation due to CuO reduction.
Figure 11 shows the morphology of the spent CuO-400 catalyst. The SEM image in Figure 11(a) indicates that the spent catalyst represents a typical aggregate morphology consisting of massive microspheres. The TEM image in Figure 11(b) shows similar morphology, and the spent catalyst exhibits much greater particle sizes than the fresh sample. As indicated in Figure 11(c), the particle size of the spent catalyst shows a broad distribution in the range of 24.5–71.2 nm. The average particle size of the spent sample is 42.5�0.5 nm, which doubles the 20.4�0.5 nm for the fresh CuO-400. The HRTEM image in Figure 11(d) reveals lattice fringes with average d-spacing of 0.254 and 0.231 nm for the (002) and (111) facets of CuO. In
addition, lattice fringes with an average d-spacing of 0.245 nm and 0.210 nm are also observed, which can be assigned to the (111) facets of Cu2O phase and the metallic Cu. This has also provided evidence for the deactivation of catalyst.
The deactivated catalyst is characterized by XPS analysis to further confirm the reduction of CuO. XPS spectra of the fresh and spent samples are presented in Figure 12, and Table 1 summarizes the surface chemical compositions of the fresh and spent samples. Figure 12(a) reveals that the Cu 2p XP profile of the spent catalyst includes two additional characteristics peaks at 952.2 eV and 932.2 eV. The observed peaks are associated with Cu 2p1/2, indicating the possible presence of Cu(+) and Cu(0) in the spent sample. Figure S6 presents the Cu LMM profile of the spent catalyst. Two characteristics peaks at 917.3 eV and 916.1 eV can be resolved from the Cu LMM curve, which can be assigned to Cu(0) and Cu(I).[16] These further confirm that the original CuO active phase has been partially reduced to Cu2O and metallic Cu in the long-term electrochemical CO2 reduction test.
The quantitative results in Table 1 show that Cu(II) and Cu(I)+Cu(0) species account for 67.92% and 32.08% in the spent sample, indicating that about one-third of the active CuO species have been reduced to Cu2O and metallic Cu in the ERC process. O 1s spectrum of the spent sample in Figure 12(b) shows a characteristic peak at 535. eV, which is assigned to the surface carbonate species (Ocs). The formation of carbonate species might be ascribed to the interaction between the adsorbed CO2 and the CuO surface. Furthermore, the formed carbonate species will cover the surface active sites, which will result in the decrease in reduction activity.
Table 1 shows that the proportions of Olat, OVs, Oads and Ocs in the spent sample are 37.30%, 31.64%, 23.88% and 7.18%, respectively. The amount of Oads in the fresh and spent samples

Most of the Olat species have been transformed to OVs and Ocs during the CO2 electrochemical reduction test, considering the reduction of CuO to Cu2O and metallic Cu and the interaction between the adsorbed CO2 and the CuO surface. This has also been evidenced by the increased concentrations of OVs and Ocs in the spent sample. Although the concentration of OVs has increased after CO2 reduction, the amount of CuO active species has decreased, and the surface active sites will be covered by the formed carbonate species, the catalyst thus will suffer deactivation in ERC process. To conclude, the increase in particle size, the loss of CuO active species and the coverage of surface active sites by carbonate species could be the primary reasons for catalyst deactivation.
One suggested strategy for reactivating the spent catalyst for reuse is the re-oxidation of the reduced sample by thermal annealing. Tan et al. also demonstrated the reduction of active CuO to Cu2O and metallic Cu in the long-term CO2RR test. The catalytic activity of the spent catalyst could be restored by thermal annealing of the used working electrode in the muffle furnace at 350 °C for 0.5 h. XRD analysis confirmed that the reduced Cu2O and metallic Cu had been re-oxidized to CuO by thermal annealing.[16] More efforts such as morphology tuning, particle size and grain boundary regulation, and surface engineering are also critically necessary in future work to improve the stability of the desired catalyst.
The ERC performance of the CuO-400 catalyst is compared to those of the copper-based catalysts reported in literatures. The testing conditions and the ERC performance of the catalysts are summarized in Table 2. Reske et al. prepared nano Cu catalysts with tunable particle size by reverse micelle method, and the selectivity of products depended on the size of the Cu NPs. The sample with an average particle size of 15.1 nm exhibited the highest FECO of 25.6%.
[23] Tang et al. synthesized polycrystal Cu NPs with a higher FECO of 34.0% using the electrodeposition method, and the reduction activity could be improved by further increasing the number of the unsaturated defect sites.[29] Huang et al. fabricated CuO NWs using the template-assisted water-bath route. Although the NWs structure was advantageous for suppressing HER, the FECO was relatively
low (23.4%), and the catalyst exhibited good selectivity toward HCOOH with a high FEHCOOH (35%–40%).
[10] Ma et al. reported that Cu NPs developed by the citrate complex method owned smaller particle sizes (7.9–15.3 nm) and exhibited a high FECO (54.7%–70.6%) at 0.6 V vs. RHE.[30] OD Cu, multi-shelled CuO and Cu NPs had also been prepared by the thermal annealing, hydrothermal, and precipitation methods, and their FECO were in the range of 22.0%–46.7%.[16,31] Xiao et al. prepared copper nanoparticles dispersed carbon aerogels (Cu/CA) by sol-gel method for ERC. The sample activated at 700 °C under CO2 and N2 atmospheres exhibited excellent CO selectivity (FECO = 75.6%). The outstanding catalytic performance was associated with the excellent textural properties, highly dispersed Cu0 on the carbon aerogels and high defect density.[32] The FECO of the desired CuO-400 catalyst reaches 48.2% at 0.93 V vs. RHE, which is higher than or comparable to those of the copperbased catalysts reported in literatures. In addition, the desired CuO-400 catalyst maintains stable catalytic activity within 2 h after the decline of current density in the initial stage. The stability of the sample is also comparable to those of the CuO and nano Cu catalysts reported by Huang et al. and Lv et al.[10,31b]

sections.heading: 3. Conclusions
sections.text:
Nanosized CuO catalysts have been synthesized by the template-assisted homogeneous precipitation method. Electrochemical CO2 reduction performance of the catalysts calcined at different temperatures has been investigated. Our results indicate that the as-synthesized CuO catalysts are capable of reducing CO2 to produce syngas with tunable CO2/H2 ratio in the range of 1 :2–2 :1. CO2 reduction activity and CO selectivity of CuO increase first and then decrease with the increase in the calcination temperature. The characterization results show that surface morphology, particle size and concentration of oxygen defects of the as-prepared CuO catalysts are dependent on the calcination temperature. CuO-200 calcined at a low temperature contains limited active species for CO2 reduction due to the incomplete decomposition of the Cu2Cl(OH)3 intermediate. CuO-300 and CuO-400 calcined at the moderate temperatures exhibit good morphology, small particle size and abundant

A further increase in calcination temperature adversely affects the catalytic activity, due to the loss of active defects caused by grain sintering. The desired CuO-400 catalyst shows good performance for CO2 reduction with a high CO faradaic efficiency of 48.2% and a great ECSA normalized CO partial current density of 1.44 mA/cm2 at 0.93 V vs. RHE. The desired CuO-400 catalyst suffers deactivation after retaining stable activity for 2 h. Catalyst deactivation is ascribed to the increase in particle size, the reduction of CuO to Cu2O and metallic Cu and the coverage of the surface active sites by the formed carbonate species. Overall, this work provides some insights into syngas production with tunable CO/H2 ratios by electrochemical CO2 reduction using CuO catalysts.

sections.heading: Preparation of Catalyst and Electrode
sections.text: Nanosized CuO catalysts were prepared by the template-assisted homogeneous precipitation method.[10] Copper chloride dihydrate (CuCl2 · 2H2O) and polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP) were employed as precursor and template, respectively. A certain gram of the precursor and the template were mixed and dissolved in 100 ml of deionized water under stirring to form a uniform solution. The mixtures were treated with ultrasound for 15 min, followed by the addition of 2 ml of NH3 ·H2O into the solution. A certain amount of NaOH solution (1 M) was added to the solution under stirring to obtain light blue precipitates. The precipitates were then filtered and washed several times using deionized water and ethanol. The precipitates were subsequently dried at 60 °C and calcined at 200– 500 °C in a muffle furnace to obtain the desired CuO catalysts. The samples calcined at varied temperatures were labeled as CuO X, where X denoted the calcination temperature. Schematic illustration of the manufacturing process of the nanostructured CuO by the template-assisted homogeneous precipitation can be found in Scheme 1 and Figure S7. CuO particles were deposited on carbon paper substrate with a geometric size of 1 cm×1 cm to form electrode for electrochemical tests. The loading of CuO on the substrate is 100 mg/cm2.

sections.heading: Catalyst Characterization
sections.text: Crystalline structures of the samples were identified by X-ray diffraction analysis (XRD, Bruker D8 Advance, Germany). Chemical functional groups of the catalysts were identified by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR, Thermo Scientific Nicolet 6700, America). Surface morphologies were investigated by fieldemission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, JSM-7800F Prime, Japan) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM, FEI Inspect F50, America). Chemical valences of the samples were identified by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo ESCALAB 250xi, America).

sections.heading: Electrochemical CO2 Reduction
sections.text:
The ERC performance of the CuO electrocatalysts were evaluated using a CHI660E workstation (CH Instruments) and a H-type electrochemical cell containing 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. Pt mesh
and Ag/AgCl were employed as a counter electrode and a reference electrode. Nafion117 proton exchange membrane (PEM) was employed to separate the cathode and anode chambers. The schematic diagram of the testing system can be found in Figure S8. N2- and CO2-staurated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolytes (0.1 M) were prepared by bubbling pure N2 or CO2 (40 ml/min) into the solution.
Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) and cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests were conducted in N2- and CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolytes under the potential of 0.93~ 0.13 V vs. RHE with a scan rate of 50 mV/s. The LSV and CV tests were performed with the consideration of 90% iR compensation. CV tests were also carried out in the non-Faradaic region under the scan rates of 5–50 mV/s to determine the electrical double-layer capacitance (Cdl) and the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA). The ECSA normalized total current density (jECSA) and partial current density of the desired products (jproduct-ECSA) can be calculated.
[33] More detailed descriptions can be found in Supporting Information. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were conducted in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte with a frequency ranging from 0.01 Hz to 106 Hz and 5 mV amplitude, in order to evaluate the charge transfer properties of the catalysts.
In chronoamperometric i-t test, CO2 was continuously supplied to the cathode chamber at 40 ml/min. The gaseous and liquid products were sampled after the test had been maintained for 60 min, in order to calculate their faradaic efficiencies (FE) under varied applied potentials. Stabilty of the desired catalyst was evaluated by sampling the products every 30 min to determine their FEs. The gaseous and liquid products were analyzed using a gas chromatography (GC) with a flame ionization detector (FID) and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). The FEs of the gaseous and liquid products were calculated by Eqs. (1) and (2) as follows:
